title: Corresponding squares
summary: For every square of one king, the square the other king must be on: the method behind opposition, triangulation and blocked pawn endings.
part.pair.title: The first pair
part.pair.summary: King and pawn against king: two squares that correspond, and whoever is to move on them loses.
part.doors.title: Two doors, one king
part.doors.summary: Separated key squares: when the black king is not on the partner, the door opens.
part.number.title: Numbering the squares
part.number.summary: The method: from the doors backwards, every white square gets a black partner.
part.tempo.title: Who has the move
part.tempo.summary: When the black king always follows, only a triangle or a spare pawn move changes who is to move.
part.lasker.title: Lasker and Reichhelm, 1901
part.lasker.summary: The most famous position of the method: a king walk along the first and second ranks.
part.game.title: Firouzja–Carlsen, 2020
part.game.summary: Opposition, close or distant, is a pair: Firouzja's defence in Stavanger, the move that was missing and when the same file does not work.
part.defend.title: The method also defends
part.defend.summary: Every square of the black king has an answer; and the recap of the lesson.
step.t_pair: King and pawn against king. The white pawn is already on c6, your king on c5 and the black one on d8, next to the queening square. If the white king picks the wrong square, the black king plants itself in front of the pawn and draws. Where does your king go?
step.t_pair.hint1: Picture the kings on d6 and d8. Is the side to move there the one in trouble?
step.t_pair.hint2: Count whose move it will be after yours, and whether the black king will still have a good square.
step.pair: d6 and d8 are a pair: corresponding squares. After 1.Kd6 the kings are on the pair with Black to move, and the black king has to leave: 1...Kc8 2.c7 and the pawn gets through. With White to move on the same pair, the pawn advances with check and the black king ends up stalemated. That is why 1.Kd6! wins: the white king reaches the pair with the black king already on the partner, and the move stays with Black. b6 and b8 are another pair, and 1.Kb6! wins too, for another reason: from d8 the black king cannot reach b8, the partner of b6. It is the trebuchet of the previous lesson, with squares instead of pawns.
step.d_pairWrong: The same pair, d6 and d8, but with White to move. See what is left.
step.d_pairWrong.m1: 1.c7+: it is my move and someone has to leave the pair. If my king steps back, the black one gets in front of the pawn; I try the advance with check.
step.d_pairWrong.m2: 1...Kc8: the black king steps onto the queening square, right in front of the pawn.
step.d_pairWrong.m3: 2.Kc6: the pawn is protected, but the black king has no move at all. Stalemate: the pair with the wrong side to move is a draw.
step.pairMove: The same start: your king on c5, the pawn on c6 and the black king on d8. Take the king to the right pair and then the pawn to a queen.
step.pairMove.done: That is it. 1.Kd6 left the move with Black; after 1...Kc8 2.c7 Kb7 3.Kd7, the pawn queens.
step.pairMove.hint: Take your king to a pair where the black king is already on the partner, so the move stays with it.
step.t_doors: A study by Grigoriev, 1924. The pawns are locked. The white king has two goals far apart: to support the advance of the d3-pawn, or to fetch the c3-pawn. The black king, on f4, seems close to everything. Where does the white king get in?
step.t_doors.hint1: From which squares does the white king support the advance of the d3-pawn? And from which squares does it attack the c3-pawn?
step.t_doors.hint2: On f4, does the black king guard those kingside squares? And if it stood on f3?
step.doors: The doors are e2 and f2, from where the king supports the advance of the d3-pawn, and a3 and b3, from where the c3-pawn falls. From f3 the black king would guard e2 and f2 at once; on f4 it guards neither. That is why 1.Ke2 (or 1.Kf2) gets in at once. The black king cannot guard both doors, and the white king picks the one that is open.
step.d_enter: The study position, with the black king on f4. Watch the door open.
step.d_enter.m1: 1.Ke2: the door. From f4 the black king does not guard e2; 1.Kf2 worked just as well.
step.d_enter.m2: 1...Kf5: the black king steps back to get in front of the d3-pawn before it moves.
step.d_enter.m3: 2.Ke3: the king stands next to d4 and supports the advance.
step.d_enter.m4: 2...Ke5: facing my king. Now the pawn can only step out with check, and the black king still blocks it.
step.d_enter.m5: 3.d4+: the pawn steps out with check, and my king stays beside it.
step.d_enter.m6: 3...Kd5: the black king blockades the d4-pawn.
step.d_enter.m7: 4.Kd3, the only move: it attacks the c3-pawn and faces the black king. It has to step back, and the c3-pawn falls; with two pawns against none on that wing, White wins.
step.enter: Your king is already on a square of the door, e2, and the black king is still on f4. But it is your move, and the king cannot stand still. Which move keeps the door?
step.enter.done: That's it. 1.Kf2 kept the door, and the black king has to leave f4. Then come 2.Ke3 and 3.d4: the technique from the demonstration.
step.enter.hint: You need to stay on a square of the door and pass the move at the same time.
step.t_number: Now the black king is on d5 and yours on c1, far from the doors. The candidates are 1.Kb1, 1.Kd1 and 1.d4, and only one wins. Which one?
step.t_number.hint1: The doors are the same: e2 and f2, a3 and b3. Which white squares threaten to get in, and which black square answers each one?
step.t_number.hint2: d1 and e1 threaten e2; e3 and f3 guard e2 and f2. c1 is next to d1 and b1; d4 is next to e3 and c5. Every white square has a black partner.
step.t_number.hint3: Count, from d5, the partner squares the black king can reach in one move. One of the three white squares has a partner out of its reach.
step.count: The arrow shows the winning move, 1.Kd1. To see why, start from the doors. d1 and e1 threaten to get in on e2; e3 and f3 guard e2 and f2. d1 is one step closer to the other door, so the partner of d1 is the black square one step closer to it: e3. That leaves e1 with f3. With the black king on the partner, White does not get in. The other pairs appear walking backwards, one at a time.
step.d_count: The white king on e1, the black one on f3, and it is my move: the pair e1 with f3. I walk to the left, and it always answers with the partner.
step.d_count.m1: 1.Kd1: eyeing the door on the left, a3 and b3.
step.d_count.m2: 1...Ke3: d1 with e3. The black king still guards e2 and f2 and gets closer to the other door.
step.d_count.m3: 2.Kc1: one more step to the left.
step.d_count.m4: 2...Kd4: c1 with d4. d4 is next to e3 just as c1 is next to d1.
step.d_count.m5: 3.Kb1: closer still to a3 and b3.
step.d_count.m6: 3...Kc5: b1 with c5. c5 is next to d4 and b4.
step.d_count.m7: 4.Ka2: now I threaten to get in on a3 or b3.
step.d_count.m8: 4...Kb4: a2 with b4, which guards a3 and b3. It never runs out of answers: with the black king always on the partner, nobody gets in, and it is a draw.
step.rule: The rule follows from the pairs. If every square of mine has a partner and the black king is always on it, it holds. So my move is to go to the square whose partner it cannot reach in one move. Here the black king is on d5, which is nobody's partner: from d5 it reaches c5 and d4, but not e3. 1.Kd1! has partner e3. 1.Kb1? has partner c5, and it goes there: draw. 1.d4? locks everything: draw. Counting the squares means this: seeing who runs out of answers first.
step.numberMove: The black king is on f3, yours on f1, and it is your move. Twice in a row: at each step of his, the partner square.
step.numberMove.done: Perfect. 1.Ke1 against f3, 2.Kd1 against e3, and now it is the black king that has to leave: when it goes to d4, the e2 door opens (3.Kc1, the partner of d4, would also win, only more slowly).
step.numberMove.hint: f3 is the partner of e1. Then e3 is the partner of d1.
step.t_tri: A study by Grigoriev. The white king's doors are e2, e3 and d4. The black king is on f3, the partner of d2: if it were Black to move, you would get in. How do you hand the move over to Black?
step.t_tri.hint1: Look for other squares of yours with the same partner as d2.
step.t_tri.hint2: Take a walk that ends on d2 with Black to move.
step.triangle: Triangulation is a case of the method too. The partner of d2 is f3, of c2 it is f4. Only b2 and b3 are as good for me as d2: they all have the same partner, f3. I have three squares with the same number and the black king has only one. I go round via c2, b3 and b2, and it cannot keep up: it is the triangle you already know, seen through corresponding squares.
step.d_tri: The whole walk, move by move.
step.d_tri.m1: 1.Kc2: I start the walk; c2 has partner f4.
step.d_tri.m2: 1...Kf4: the black king goes to the partner, as it must.
step.d_tri.m3: 2.Kb3: a square with the same partner as d2, f3.
step.d_tri.m4: 2...Kf3: it follows again, to the partner of b3.
step.d_tri.m5: 3.Kb2: one more square with partner f3. I changed square without changing number; the black king has no other square with the number of f3.
step.d_tri.m6: 3...Kf4: it has to leave f3 and picks the partner of c2.
step.d_tri.m7: 4.Kc2: the pair c2 with f4, now with Black to move. The walk changed who is to move.
step.d_tri.m8: 4...Kf3: the black king has to leave the partner.
step.d_tri.m9: 5.Kd2: the starting position, with Black to move. After 5...Kf4, 6.Ke2 gets in through the door.
step.d_corner: Now another structure, from a training position. The white king wants to reach b7 through the corner, and the black king follows on the other side of the b6-pawn.
step.d_corner.m1: 1.Ka6: via the corner, on the way to a7 and b7.
step.d_corner.m2: 1...Kc6: a6 with c6. From c6 the black king guards b7.
step.d_corner.m3: 2.Ka7: one more step towards the corner.
step.d_corner.m4: 2...Kc7: a7 with c7, and b7 and b8 are still guarded.
step.d_corner.m5: 3.Ka8: the corner. It goes no deeper; the other square is back on a6.
step.d_corner.m6: 3...Kc8: a8 with c8. Here there is no triangle: each square of mine has a single partner. And the a4-pawn has no free step, because 4.a5 is captured by 4...bxa5. The move never changes hands, and it is a draw. A pawn with a spare step would play the part of the triangle.
step.triMove: Back to Grigoriev's study: the black king on f3, the partner of d2, and it is your move. Make the walk that hands over the move.
step.triMove.done: That is it. With 2.Kb3 and 3.Kb2 you spent a move without changing pair; from here, 4.Kc2 and 5.Kd2 leave the move with Black.
step.triMove.hint: Three squares of yours have the same partner, f3.
step.t_lasker: Lasker and Reichhelm composed this position in 1901. Nine pieces, everything locked, and the white king in the corner. It has two doors: b5, on the queenside, and h5, on the kingside. What is the first move?
step.t_lasker.hint1: The white king has three squares. For each one, find its partner and see whether the black king, from a7, reaches it in one move.
step.t_lasker.hint2: The black king will answer your first move with a square on the seventh or eighth rank. Pick a square whose partner is out of its reach.
step.laskerKeys: Two doors again, further apart. On the left, c4 threatens to enter on b5 and win the a5-pawn; the partner of c4 is b6. On the right, the king goes via e3, f3, g3 and h4 to h5, and the f5-pawn falls; the black king needs to be on d7 or d8 when I reach e3. Between the doors, the pairs the line needs: b3, d3, b1 and d1 have partner c7; c3 and c1 have partner b7; d2 has partner c8; c2 has partner b8. The black king on a7 is on nobody's partner square, and the move is the square whose partner it cannot reach: 1.Kb1.
step.d_lasker: The white king's walk, move by move.
step.d_lasker.m1: 1.Kb1, the only winning move. The partner of b1 is c7, and from a7 the black king cannot reach c7.
step.d_lasker.m2: 1...Kb7: b7 is the partner of c1 and c3.
step.d_lasker.m3: 2.Kc1: the partner of b7, with Black to move. They have to leave.
step.d_lasker.m4: 2...Kc7: the partner of b1 and d1.
step.d_lasker.m5: 3.Kd1: the right partner again, and again it is their move.
step.d_lasker.m6: 3...Kd8: the black king keeps an eye on the door on the right.
step.d_lasker.m7: 4.Kc2, whose partner is b8. From d8 you cannot reach b8.
step.d_lasker.m8: 4...Kc8: the black king goes to the partner of d2.
step.d_lasker.m9: 5.Kd2: the partner of c8, and it is their move.
step.d_lasker.m10: 5...Kd7: still eyeing the door on the right.
step.d_lasker.m11: 6.Kc3, partner of b7. From d7 you cannot reach b7.
step.d_lasker.m12: 6...Kc7: the partner of d3, the square I am going to now. There was nothing else left.
step.d_lasker.m13: 7.Kd3: the partner of c7, for the third time with Black to move. Now the answers have run out: if the black king goes to b6 or b7, I run to the right, via e3, f3, g3 and h4, to h5; if it goes anywhere else, I get in via c4 and b5.
step.laskerMove.done: That is it: 1.Kb1 and 2.Kc1, the two only moves. From there it is the walk of the demonstration, pair by pair, until the black king runs out of answers. When it escapes to b6, the white king runs via e3, f3 and g3 to h5, and the f5-pawn falls.
step.laskerMove.hint: The partner of b1 is c7, and the black king on a7 cannot get there. Then answer b7 with its partner square.
step.t_game: This is the ending of Alireza Firouzja against Magnus Carlsen, in round nine of Norway Chess 2020, in Stavanger. In a knight against bishop ending, Carlsen took the h5-pawn with his knight, 60...Nxh5+, and after 61.Bxh5 Kxh5 he went into this pawn ending a pawn up. White defends: if the black king gets through on the queenside to d4, the e4-pawn falls. Firouzja held for seven moves, always with the right square. Carlsen has just played 68...Kd6. Where does the white king go?
step.t_game.hint1: Until now, White answered every step of the black king with a square on the same file.
step.t_game.hint2: If the black king goes to c5, you need to be ready to answer with c3. Staying on d3 is impossible, because it is your move.
step.game: The pairs of this game lie on the same file: d6 with d2, c5 with c3, b5 with b3. On the d-file there are three squares between the kings, the distant opposition; on the c- and b-files, a single square, the close opposition. d4 does not work, because the e5-pawn guards it. Against d6, only 69.Kd2! drew: from d2 the white king still reaches c3 when the black one goes to c5. Firouzja played 69.Kc3?, one step too early, and after 69...Kc5 he resigned. That the pair lies on the same file belongs to this structure, it is not a rule: with other pawns, it can jump files.
step.d_game: The moves of the game, from move 65. The black king looks for a way to the queenside, and the white one answers each of its steps. In this structure the square on the same file always works; at the end of the part you will see another one where it draws.
step.d_game.m1: 65.Kf2: on the file of the black king, which is on f8. 65.Kf3 also held: the black king is still far from c5, and White has some slack.
step.d_game.m2: 65...Ke7: the black king heads for the centre.
step.d_game.m3: 66.Ke2: again on the same file. Here 66.Ke1 and 66.Ke3 also worked.
step.d_game.m4: 66...Ke8: a step back, trying to pass the move.
step.d_game.m5: 67.Ke3: still on the e-file. The slack shrinks: only 67.Ke1 worked as well.
step.d_game.m6: 67...Kd7: now along the d-file, heading for c5 and b4.
step.d_game.m8: 68...Kd6: the black king has reached the door to the queenside. Against d6, only one square holds.
step.gameError: After 69.Kc3?, the pair belongs to Black: 69...Kc5, and now it is the white king that has to leave c3. In the game, Firouzja resigned here. The arrows show why: 70.Kd3 Kb4 71.Kd2 Kc4 72.Ke3 Kc3 73.Ke2 Kd4, and the black king reaches d4 from the other side; the e4-pawn falls.
step.gameMove: The game position, after 68...Kd6. Do what Firouzja did not: hold the draw for the next three moves.
step.gameMove.done: That is it. With 69.Kd2! and then c3 against c5, b3 against b5, the black king does not get through. That was Firouzja's draw.
step.gameMove.hint: Against d6, the square on the same file from which you still reach c3 when the black king goes to c5.
step.gameFar: Another structure, a made-up one: pawns on c3 and d4 against d5, your king on e1 and the black one on d6. Here, close to the pawns, following the black king on the same file draws: the pairs do not line up, they jump two files. d6 pairs with the f-file, e6 with the g-file. Win with White over the next two moves.
step.gameFar.done: That is it. Against d6, 1.Kf2! Against 1...Ke6, 2.Kg2! Always two files to the side, never on its file: there, 1.Kd2? and 2.Ke2? drew.
step.gameFar.hint: Against the black king on d6, your king goes to the f-file; against e6, to the g-file.
step.t_defend: Now you defend, in a training position. The black king will choose a road: through the middle, via e7 and e6, or along the edge, via g7 and g6, with the h5-pawn behind it. Which square of the white king answers both roads?
step.t_defend.hint1: 1.Kf2, 1.Kf4 and 1.Ke4 lose: on each of them the black king picks the road your king cannot reach.
step.defend: The method also defends. The pairs you need: f8 with g2, e7 with h3, f7 with g3. The odd one is the first: against the black king in the middle of the eighth rank, the white king steps back. 1.Kg2! is the only move that holds. From g2 it answers e7 with h3 and f7 with g3, and never runs out of answers.
step.defendMove: Answer each square of the black king with its partner.
step.defendMove.done: That's it. 1.Kg2, 2.Kh3 and 3.Kg3: every square of the black king had its answer. As long as it stays that way, it does not get in.
step.defendMove.hint: Against f8, g2. Against e7, h3. Against f7, g3.
step.recap: Three rules to take with you. First: start from the doors, the key squares; the squares next to them form the first pairs. Second: a square next to two numbered squares is the partner of the square on the other side next to the same numbers; that is how the pairs walk backwards. Third: on your move, go to the square whose partner the other king cannot reach; if it always can, it is a draw, and that is how the method defends. Opposition, close or distant, and triangulation are cases of this method: in the opposition the partners line up; in triangulation you have more squares with the same number than your opponent, and a spare pawn move plays the same part.
step.finish: Now play to the end. The black king is on b5, yours on c1, and it is your move. Find the square whose partner it cannot reach, get in through the door and convert.
key.grigoriev: Grigoriev, 1924: the white king has two entry doors, far apart, and the black king can't guard both at once.
key.method: The method at work: for every square of the black king there is one right square for the white king. White goes to the only one the black king can't answer.
key.roschMast: Rösch against Mast, 1995: White draws by answering every step of the black king with the matching square, always beside it.
key.triangle: A study by Grigoriev: the white king has three squares that answer the same square of the black king, and so it can lose a tempo. This is triangulation seen through corresponding squares.
key.lasker: The method's most famous position, by Lasker and Reichhelm, 1901: the white king takes a long, patient walk until it forces its way in, and White wins.
key.defend: The method works in defence too: for every step of the black king, the white king answers with the matching square, and the draw is safe.
history: In some pawn endings the kings stand facing each other, away from the pawns, in a waiting dance: whoever puts a foot wrong loses. The opposition explains the simple cases, but not all of them. For the rest there is the method of corresponding squares: for every square the enemy king can go to, there is one right square for your king. It's an ending that looks like a matter of patience and is really a matter of calculation, and even books have got it wrong. The most famous position dates from 1901, composed by Emanuel Lasker, then world champion, and the American Gustavus Reichhelm. And there's a lovely curiosity: in 1932 the painter Marcel Duchamp, who was also a chess master, wrote a whole book on this subject with Vitaly Halberstadt.
practice: Now the real ending: the black king on b5, yours on c1, and it is your move. Find the square whose partner it cannot reach, get in through the door and win. Pick your pace and go.
ex.e01: King and pawn against king: the simplest pairs of the method. Find the winning move.
ex.e01.hint: The partner of c6 is c8. From e8, can the black king get there?
ex.e01.solution: 1.Kc6! The partner of c6 is c8, and from e8 the black king cannot reach c8. After 1...Kd8, 2.d7!, the black king has to go to e7 and 3.Kc7 takes the pawn through. 1.Kd5? allows 1...Kd8, the pair with me to move, and draws; 1.d7+? draws too.
ex.e02: Doubled pawns on the b-file, and the black king in front of them. Where does the white king go? Find the winning move.
ex.e02.hint: c4 and b6 are a pair: whoever arrives first, with the other able to answer, has to step back. Wait on a square next to c4.
ex.e02.solution: 1.Kd4! (1.Kd3 and 1.Kb3 also win): c4 and b6 are the pair, and the white king waits beside it. After 1...Kb6, 2.Kc4!, and it is the black king that has to leave; if 1...Kc7, 2.Kc5. 1.Kc4? at once allows 1...Kb6!, and it is you who steps back: draw. 1.b6? draws as well.
ex.e03: The a6-pawn is stuck, and the black king wants a7. Find the draw.
ex.e03.hint: 1.Kb5? takes the king towards c6, but 1...Ka7! and the a6-pawn falls first. Look for the partner square of b8.
ex.e03.solution: 1.Kb4!, the partner of b8; nothing else holds. After 1...Ka8, 2.Kc4 (or 2.Ka4), and when the black king returns to b8, 3.Kb4 again. 1.Kb5?, 1.Ka3?, 1.Kb3? and 1.a7+? lose.
ex.e04: A training position by miguel_angel_jodraza. A pawn up, but the white king is in the corner and the black one close to everything. Only one move wins.
ex.e04.hint: On the f- and g-files the distant opposition rules: g1 with g7, f1 with f7, g2 with g8 and g6, f2 with f8 and f6. On the d- and e-files, next to the pawns, the pairs vanish. Stay on the right files.
ex.e04.solution: 1.Kg1!, the distant opposition on the g-file (1.Kg2? allows 1...Kg8 or 1...Kg6; 1.Kh2? and 1.c5? draw as well). After 1...Kf7, 2.Kf1!, the partner of f7. If the black king runs to e7, 3.Kg2 (or 3.Kg1): from e7 it cannot get back to g8, g6 or g7, and the opposition is yours for good. 3.Ke1? or 3.Ke2? behind it draw: on the e-file the pair does not hold.
ex.e06: A training position by Strategically_Endgam. The black king guards b6, c7 and c5. Only one move wins.
ex.e06.hint: The white king goes round through the corner: the pairs are a6 with c6 and a7 with c7. The spare tempo of the a3-pawn decides who has the move; spend it at the right moment.
ex.e06.solution: 1.Ka6! (1.a4?, 1.c5?, 1.Ka4? and 1.Kb4? draw). After 1...Kc6, 2.a4! The spare tempo, spent now, leaves the black king to move (2.Ka7? allows 2...b5 and draws). After 2...Kc7, 3.Ka7!, the partner of c7; after 3...Kc6, 4.Kb8 (or 4.Ka6, 4.Ka8), and the white king reaches b7 and takes the pawns. If 1...Kb8 right at the start, 2.Kxb6.
ex.e07: The white king will go round along the eighth rank looking for a key square. Each of your moves is the only one that holds. Hold the draw.
ex.e07.hint: f6 is a key square for White too: if the white king reaches e6 while yours is far from g6, the f6-pawn falls. Think in pairs: for each square of the white king on the way to e6 there is a right square for yours. The first move is not the natural one.
ex.e07.solution: 1...Kh6!! It looks like running away, but it is the right pair. From then on your king copies White's: 2.Kc7 Kg7, 3.Kb7 Kh7, 4.Kb8 Kh8, 5.Kc8 Kg8, 6.Kd7 Kh7 and, when it reaches e6, 7...Kg6!, guarding f6. At every move only that one draws; 1...f5? always loses. Karsten Müller and Frank Lamprecht's example.
